terms.definition: Software Development Lifecycle — the structured set of phases (Requirements, Design, Development, Testing, Deployment, Monitoring) every software product goes through, repeating continuously.
terms.example: Like a product roadmap that never truly ends — once you deploy, monitoring feeds back into new requirements.

terms.definition: A linear SDLC methodology where each phase must completely finish before the next begins, with requirements frozen at the start and no ability to go back.
terms.example: Building an entire car from scratch before ever showing it to the customer — and only then discovering they wanted a truck.

terms.definition: An iterative software development methodology where work is divided into short sprints (1–2 weeks), delivering working software at the end of each cycle with continuous customer feedback.
terms.example: Like quarterly exams instead of one annual exam — smaller cycles, faster feedback, better final results.

terms.definition: A short, time-boxed iteration in Agile (typically 1–2 weeks) during which the team plans, builds, and delivers a working increment of software.
terms.example: A development team takes a 'User Login' feature, builds it, tests it, and delivers it within one 2-week sprint.

terms.definition: A culture and set of practices that bridges the gap between development and operations by automating deployment, standardizing environments, and promoting shared responsibility.
terms.example: Instead of Dev throwing code over a wall to Ops, both teams collaborate with automated pipelines, shared dashboards, and joint accountability.

terms.definition: The practice of automatically testing and building code every time a developer commits changes to the shared repository, stopping the pipeline immediately if anything fails.
terms.example: Developer pushes code → Jenkins triggers → Maven builds → JUnit tests run → SonarQube scans → pipeline reports pass or fail.

terms.definition: A CD practice where code is always in a deployable state after passing all automated tests, but a human must manually approve before the final push to production.
terms.example: The new feature is tested, packaged, and sitting in JFrog ready to go live — the manager reviews the report and clicks 'Deploy' at midnight.

terms.definition: A CD practice where code automatically deploys to production with no human approval if all automated tests pass.
terms.example: Developer merges a bug fix → all 500 tests pass → pipeline deploys to production automatically — no approval needed, live in minutes.

terms.definition: An open-source CI/CD orchestration tool that connects and coordinates all pipeline tools (Maven, JUnit, SonarQube, JFrog) into a single automated workflow triggered by code commits.
terms.example: Like a conductor in an orchestra — Jenkins doesn't play instruments; it tells Maven, JUnit, and SonarQube when to play.

terms.definition: A Java build tool that compiles source code and packages it with all its dependencies into a deployable artifact (JAR or WAR file).
terms.example: Think of Maven as a chef that takes raw ingredients (source code + libraries) and produces a finished dish (deployable package).

terms.definition: A static code analysis tool that scans source code for security vulnerabilities, bugs, code smells, and test coverage — without running the code.
terms.example: SonarQube finds a SQL injection vulnerability in the code before it ever reaches production, preventing a potential data breach.

terms.definition: Java Code Coverage tool that measures what percentage of source code lines are executed by the automated test suite.
terms.example: If you wrote 1,000 lines of code and your tests only run through 700 lines, JaCoCo reports 70% coverage.

terms.definition: An automated checkpoint in the CI/CD pipeline that stops deployment if code does not meet defined quality thresholds (coverage percentage, security grade, number of critical bugs).
terms.example: Quality Gate configured: if coverage < 80% or security grade < A, block the pipeline. Code with 65% coverage automatically fails.

terms.definition: An artifact repository that stores and versions built deployment packages, enabling teams to roll back to any previous version instantly if a deployment fails.
terms.example: Version 2.1.5 of the app is deployed and breaks production. Team rolls back to version 2.1.4 stored in JFrog — back online in 2 minutes.

terms.definition: A separate Git branch where a developer writes and tests their own code in isolation before merging into the main branch, which triggers the CI/CD pipeline.
terms.example: Developer creates branch 'feature/user-auth', builds the login system, tests it, then opens a pull request to merge to main.

terms.definition: The problem where code works in the developer's local environment but fails in production because of differing OS versions, software versions, or configuration settings.
terms.example: Developer uses Node.js 18 on Windows. Production server runs Node.js 14 on Linux. Application breaks in production.

terms.definition: The practice of managing cloud infrastructure — servers, networks, databases — using version-controlled code files instead of manual console configuration.
terms.example: A Terraform file describes a VPC with 3 subnets, 2 EC2 instances, and 1 RDS database. Running the file creates all resources automatically.

terms.definition: An open-source IaC tool for provisioning and managing cloud infrastructure across AWS, Azure, and GCP using declarative configuration files.
terms.example: Terraform code: 'create an EC2 t2.micro in us-east-1 inside VPC xyz' — one command creates the entire resource.

terms.definition: A configuration management and automation tool used to install software, update packages, and manage configuration across many servers simultaneously using playbooks.
terms.example: Ansible playbook: 'install Node.js 18 and Nginx on all 50 production servers' — runs against all servers in parallel with one command.

terms.definition: The process of reverting a production deployment to a previous, known-good version when a new deployment causes errors or failures.
terms.example: New version deployed at 2 PM; monitoring shows 500 errors at 2:05 PM; team rolls back to previous artifact in JFrog — site healthy by 2:08 PM.

terms.definition: The DevOps cultural principle that both development and operations teams are jointly accountable for software quality, deployment reliability, and production health — eliminating the blame game.
terms.example: Instead of Dev saying 'we built it' and Ops saying 'it broke on our servers,' both teams see the same metrics and fix issues together.

terms.definition: A project management tool used in Agile teams to write user stories, create and assign tasks, organize sprints, and track work status (To Do / In Progress / Done).
terms.example: Sprint board in Jira: 5 stories planned, 3 in progress, 2 done — visible to the entire team including QA, developers, and product owner.
